title: Suncorp has held preliminary talks with suitor
full_text:
Suncorp is understood to have entered preliminary discussions with its suitor, Tokio Marine, and executives from the company have travelled to Japan for the talks, sources say.
DataRoom reported at the weekend that Tokio Marine’s focus for embarking on a buyout of one of Australia’s largest insurance firms had narrowed to Suncorp, although earlier suggestions were that rival IAG was equally under consideration.
It is understood that as of last week there had yet to be any formal inbound proposal.
Suncorp, based in Brisbane, is Australia’s second-largest insurance firm and has a market value of $20bn.
When approached by DataRoom the company declined to comment on the speculation. The understanding is that among those who had travelled to Tokyo over recent weeks – where Tokio Marine is based – was chief financial officer Jeremy Robson, who has been acting chief executive while Steve Johnston was absent on medical leave.
“There has been engagement,” said one source with knowledge of the developments. Tokio Marine is one of the largest insurance firms globally and has reinsurance deals with both Suncorp and IAG.
In March, Berkshire Hathaway announced it had purchased a 2.5 per cent stake in Tokio Marine Holdings for $US1.8bn ($2.6bn), forming a strategic partnership that would include collaboration in reinsurance and potential acquisitions, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. It would not acquire more than a 9.9 per cent stake without prior approval from Tokio Marine’s board.
An insurance industry expert said that Australia was an attractive market in that it was largely a duopoly comprising IAG and Suncorp.
However, insurers were expensive relative to those overseas, and many global insurance giants had taken the view that they could gain exposure to the market and gain the same benefits through reinsurance deals.
Among the world’s largest insurance giants, Tokio Marine and Munich RE were the only reinsurers that bought direct-insurance firms.
Berkshire Hathaway’s former billionaire chairman and chief executive, Warren Buffett, had taken the view that he did not want to own general insurance firms outside the US.
Mr Buffett stepped down from the board this year, meaning his views are no longer part of the formal decision-making process.
Sources tempered the speculation, saying that talks were in early stages and may not eventuate in a deal.
Berkshire Hathaway was considered a value buyer, meaning Tokio Marine and Suncorp may not agree on price.
Sources said that if a deal were to happen, it would come towards the end of Mr Johnston’s Suncorp tenure. He was appointed to the top job in 2019.
As reported by DataRoom at the weekend, investment bankers at Suncorp’s defence adviser, JPMorgan, were thought to be preparing for a highly anticipated inbound buyout proposal for Suncorp, while Goldman Sachs was also busy on an insurance deal, and was believed to be working with Tokio Marine.
DataRoom first reported in July that Tokio Marine was undertaking work on potential acquisition targets in Australia. It sent representatives to Australia in August to carry out further exploratory work for a potential $20bn-plus purchase of one of Australia’s top insurance firms.
It is understood that the Japanese financial group had executives on the ground, meeting with representatives of Insurance Australia Group and Suncorp, along with other industry experts in what was understood to be detailed analysis of the two potential targets and the sector.
Tokio Marine wants to embark on a transaction to put excess capital to work, and analysts say it told the market about four months ago it wanted to break into the Australian or Canadian markets with a major acquisition.
Founded in 1879, Tokio Marine operates in more than 50 countries and regions. It has more than 50,000 employees worldwide. Insurers globally are reaping a windfall from inflation-fuelled price increases, justified partly by the threat of catastrophic events brought on by climate change. As a result, they have enjoyed near-record profits and prospered on the back of higher interest rates, as their cash holdings generate more earnings.
